title: 7 of the Most Haunted Homes in Alabama: Ghosts, Legends, and Stories That Will Give You Chills!
excerpt: Happy Halloween, Alabama. And if you believe in ghosts, may yours be friendly ones.
content:
Halloween weekend is here, and if there’s one thing Alabama has plenty of besides football, sweet tea, and Southern hospitality, it’s a good ghost story!

Get our free mobile app

Our state has a fascinating history, dating back hundreds of years. We’ve got antebellum mansions, old plantation homes, historic hotels, and buildings where generations of Alabamians have lived and died.

And according to local legends, some of those former residents may not have ever left!

From mysterious lights in a Tuscaloosa mansion to the ghost of a wealthy banker who supposedly refuses to leave his former home, Alabama has some pretty interesting haunted-house stories.

So, in the spirit of Halloween, let’s take a look at seven of Alabama’s most talked-about haunted historic homes. You might want to leave a light on tonight!

1. The Drish House – Tuscaloosa

If we’re talking about haunted homes in Alabama, we have to start right here in Tuscaloosa.

The historic Drish House, built in the 1830s by physician John R. Drish, is probably one of the state’s most famous haunted locations.

The most famous story involves Sarah Drish, the wife of the home’s original owner.

According to legend, after John Drish died in 1867, Sarah became fascinated with the candles used during his funeral. She reportedly wanted those same candles used at her own funeral someday.

When Sarah died in 1884, however, the candles couldn’t be found.

And that’s where things get interesting.

Legend says mysterious lights began appearing in the home’s third-story tower, sometimes resembling flames. The stories became so popular that the Drish House was featured in Kathryn Tucker Windham’s famous book, 13 Alabama Ghosts and Jeffrey.

Visitors have also reported strange noises, slamming doors, and the sound of children laughing when nobody else is around.

Some people believe Sarah Drish is still keeping an eye on her old home.

2. The Gorgas House – Tuscaloosa

Here’s another Tuscaloosa location with a reputation for unusual activity.

Located on the University of Alabama campus, the Gorgas House dates back to 1829 and has served several purposes over its long history.

But its most famous resident was Amelia Gayle Gorgas, affectionately known as the mother of the University.

And according to stories shared by museum employees and visitors, she may still be around.

Some staff members have reported seeing a woman resembling Amelia wearing her green obituary dress.

Others describe hearing footsteps climbing the stairs, followed by the sound of a dress swishing across the floor.

There’s even a story about Amelia’s music box apparently playing without anyone winding it.

Perhaps the most interesting detail is that the university has embraced these stories as part of the home’s history, offering special haunted tours.

Apparently, even after all these years, Mrs. Gorgas may still be looking after the students!

3. Spring Villa Mansion – Opelika

This one comes with a particularly creepy detail: the 13th step.

Spring Villa Mansion, also known as the Penn Yonge House, dates back to approximately 1850 and sits inside Spring Villa Park near Opelika.

According to local legend, the original owner, William Penn Yonge, was murdered by an enslaved person who reportedly hid in a small space alongside the mansion’s spiral staircase.

The story claims Yonge was stabbed as he climbed the stairs and died on the 13th step.

For years, visitors reportedly pointed to a dark reddish stain on that particular step.

Some believed it was blood.

The city of Opelika acknowledges that the story is a legend and that its details cannot be established as fact.

Still, the 13th step has become part of the mansion’s spooky reputation.

Would you walk up that staircase alone at midnight?

I think I’ll pass!

4. Sturdivant Hall – Selma

This beautiful Greek Revival mansion may look like something straight out of a Southern history book, but it has a rather unsettling story attached to it.

Built in 1852, Sturdivant Hall eventually became the home of wealthy banker John Parkman.

Parkman later found himself in serious financial and legal trouble. He was arrested and imprisoned after authorities investigated the bank’s financial problems.

In 1867, he was killed while attempting to escape prison.

But according to local legend, before his death, Parkman vowed that he would never leave his home until his name was cleared.

And some people believe he kept his promise!

Visitors and museum employees have reported unexplained footsteps and strange sounds coming from the upstairs portion of the house.

The story of John Parkman’s ghost even made its way into Kathryn Tucker Windham’s 13 Alabama Ghosts and Jeffrey.

Apparently, some homeowners simply refuse to move out!

5. Gaines Ridge Dinner Club – Camden

Now, this one might be especially interesting because you can reportedly enjoy a good meal while sharing the building with a few unexpected guests!

Gaines Ridge Dinner Club is located inside an antebellum home dating back to the 1820s.

The historic property is famous for its food, but its reputation for paranormal activity has also attracted plenty of attention.

One of the most frequently mentioned spirits is a tall, thin, bearded man dressed in black, believed by some to be a former owner named Ebenezer Hearn.

Other stories involve a mysterious woman who supposedly floats past the windows.

Guests and employees have also reported hearing the cries of a baby and smelling pipe smoke in rooms where nobody is smoking.

Imagine enjoying your dinner, looking toward the window, and seeing someone staring back at you who isn’t supposed to be there!

Gaines Ridge has earned a reputation as one of Alabama’s most unusual dining destinations.

Just remember to save a seat for the unexpected guests!

6. Jemison-Van de Graaff Mansion – Tuscaloosa

We’re making another stop in Tuscaloosa, where one of Alabama’s most beautiful historic mansions has developed a reputation for some unusual occurrences.

Built between 1859 and 1862 for Alabama Senator Robert Jemison Jr., this magnificent Italianate mansion was considered technologically advanced for its time.

Today, it’s a historic museum and event venue.

But according to people associated with the property, not every visitor may be alone when walking through its rooms.

Stories include unexplained breezes, mysterious orbs, strange noises, and shadows appearing in windows.

One particularly interesting legend involves the spirit of a young girl who reportedly died in the house. Some believe her presence can occasionally be seen near the main staircase.

There is also a tragic history involving Colonel Andrew Coleman Hargrove, who died in the mansion.

Whether you believe in ghosts or not, it’s easy to understand why a house with this much history inspires such stories.

7. Richards-DAR House – Mobile

Our final stop takes us to Mobile, where the Richards-DAR House has its own collection of spooky stories.

Built in 1860 for Captain Charles G. Richards and his wife, Caroline, this beautiful historic home is known for its elaborate ironwork, beautiful interiors, and fascinating architecture.

But some of the stories associated with the property are a little less elegant!

Paranormal accounts associated with the home include reports of children laughing and playing near the staircase, a mysterious woman appearing in an upstairs window, and a man dressed in Victorian clothing seemingly sitting in the parlor.

There have also been stories about unexplained piano music, doors opening and closing, and marbles moving around in an upstairs bedroom.

The house is now a museum operated by local Daughters of the American Revolution chapters and has even hosted special haunted tours.

Apparently, some of its former residents may still enjoy entertaining visitors!

So, Are Alabama’s Haunted Houses Really Haunted?

That’s the million-dollar question!

Are these places actually inhabited by spirits, or are the stories simply the result of old buildings, unusual noises, and imaginations running wild?

We may never know.

But there’s something fascinating about these old Alabama homes. Each one has a history, and behind every history is a collection of people, families, tragedies, celebrations, and sometimes unexplained events.

Perhaps that’s why ghost stories have survived for generations.

We love a good mystery, especially when it comes with a little Southern history.

And here’s something to remember this Halloween weekend: You don’t have to travel to Salem, Massachusetts, or spend a fortune visiting a haunted attraction to get a good scare.

Some of the best ghost stories might be right here in our own backyard.

So, if you happen to hear footsteps upstairs tonight when everyone else is downstairs, or see a mysterious light in an old window, don’t be too quick to investigate.

It might just be an old Alabama resident checking in!

Happy Halloween, Alabama. And if you believe in ghosts, may yours be friendly ones.
